name: Somewhere to Land
tagline: You hardly crack a smile. You're having the best time in the room.
epigraph: Named after a regular, mixed by the bartender. The regular denied being its author.
glassware: large plain tumbler (about 350 ml), three ice cubes
language_row: Wren's Resonance on reading v2: ready. Recognised, not flattered: the friend with both arms going, one word from the guest, and the table going; "They get the laugh. It comes off you." "This is me": "People think you put up with the loudest person at the table. You picked them." Sceptic: "you make people laugh" fits the whole family; the laugh coming off the quiet one, needing the friend to be ridiculous, and the fear of being taken for the grown-up who doesn't get it narrow it to this one. Fenced out: the Morale Booster, the Tease's timing, the Alternative Comic's straight face, the Naïf's eyebrow, the Stand-up's "everybody"; the Nanny's "sensible one" and measures (the lime is never measured); *Word Gets Round*'s phrases and its lime-or-lemon. The drink gives each partner a part: the bar's rye, the colonel's reportedly favourite water, and the lime they both ended up with. Williamson's pleasure is signposted twice. Pronoun warnings accepted: "he"/"his" are Rickey and Williamson. ✓
sources: Studio fact card `_studio/fact-cards/george-williamson-joe-rickey.md` (extends `bobby-heugel-lime-crisis-2014.md`): Oxford Companion, RICKEY (pdf 1661–1664) and SHOOMAKER'S (pdf 1789–1790), Derek Brown; Wondrich, *Imbibe!* pdf 117–119; Regan, *The Joy of Mixology* (2018) pdf 376, quoting Crockett (1935). *The Culinary Craft* (1915), an archive.org OCR highlight only, unread in full and kept out. Drink: *Cocktail Codex* p. 211 (Highball), p. 4. Room notes: `work/jester-ruler/`.
names_note: **Name split three ways; Robin's call.** Wren: *Somewhere to Land* (names what this person gives, and the phrase isn't spent in the reading). Tomás: *Dry Wit* (the person's humour, and the glass's truth: no sugar, rye's dryness; he could take *Don't Look at Me*). Hester: *Don't Look at Me* (Rickey's "not the author" as the guest's own deadpan line; she notes Wren and Tomás both said they could take it). The pour carries Wren's title-block name until Robin picks. Also considered: *Not the Author*, *The Feed*, *Second Banana* (a banana on the menu with no banana in the glass).
open_items: **Flag: the name.** Three-way split at the round-4 vote (Wren *Somewhere to Land*, Tomás *Dry Wit*, Hester *Don't Look at Me*). Everything else is signed by all three.

**Who invented the Rickey is contested** (Rickey's own accounts vary; Brown 1930 names Williamson; Oxford lists a stranger with limes). The lime is told per telling: in Rickey's own, one of the bartenders; in Brown's, a stranger handed Williamson the limes (Hester's L1, round 4). Williamson's enjoyment is "I like to think".

**Apollinaris is "reportedly" the colonel's water** (Oxford pdf 1663), recommended by name; any plain sparkling mineral water works. Its label is unverified for 2026 (the library dates it to about 2014); plain (unflavoured) holds the veto-free floor.

**Owned near-miss:** *Word Gets Round* (regular-guy) is a bourbon Rickey. Ours differs in five places: rye, the colonel's mineral water, half a lime by eye with the shell in, three cubes, a large tumbler. The category is shared; the cocktail isn't.
**Rye's dryness** is Tomás's taste inference, not the *Codex*'s. Rye is the bar's (Shoomaker's had its own brand, pdf 1789), never a named bottle.
**Kept out on purpose:** "Dont Drink too Many", Rickey's death and money troubles, the Confederate service, the gambling room, the health talk, the 1915 headline.
